_about: Hand-written descriptions for tree groups (muscles split into parts, organ groups) and key surface regions without a Wikipedia text. See app/extra_content.py.

Masseter.description:
The most powerful muscle of mastication: a thick quadrilateral muscle from the zygomatic arch to the lateral surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible, in a superficial and a deep part. It elevates the mandible to clench the teeth and can be felt contracting just in front of the angle of the jaw.
It is supplied by the masseteric nerve (mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve) through the mandibular notch; the parotid duct crosses its surface a finger's breadth below the zygomatic arch.

Lateral pterygoid muscle.description:
Short, thick muscle of mastication in the infratemporal fossa with two heads: the superior from the infratemporal surface of the greater wing of the sphenoid, the inferior from the lateral pterygoid plate. It inserts into the pterygoid fovea of the mandibular neck and the articular disc and capsule of the temporomandibular joint.
It is the only muscle of mastication that opens the mouth, by drawing the condyle and disc forward onto the articular eminence; acting alternately, the two sides produce grinding movements. Supplied by the mandibular nerve.

Biceps femoris muscle.description:
The lateral hamstring. Its long head arises from the ischial tuberosity with semitendinosus, its short head from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line; the common tendon inserts on the head of the fibula, where it can be felt as the lateral border of the popliteal fossa.
It flexes the knee and laterally rotates the flexed leg, and the long head extends the hip. The long head is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, the short head by the common fibular division. The common fibular nerve runs along its medial border.

Quadriceps femoris muscle.description:
The great extensor of the knee, filling the anterior compartment of the thigh: rectus femoris (which also crosses and flexes the hip) and vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius. Their tendons converge on the quadriceps tendon, which encloses the patella and continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
It is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4); the knee jerk tests L3-L4. It stabilises the knee in standing, climbing and landing, and wastes quickly after knee injury or immobilisation.

Triceps surae muscle.description:
The calf muscle group: the two heads of gastrocnemius and the soleus, joined by the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon to the back of the calcaneus. It is the main plantarflexor of the ankle, providing push-off in walking, running and jumping; gastrocnemius also flexes the knee.
Supplied by the tibial nerve (S1-S2), tested by the ankle jerk. Its contraction squeezes the deep veins (calf muscle pump), which is why immobility predisposes to deep vein thrombosis.

Rotator cuff muscles.description:
Four short scapulohumeral muscles whose tendons blend with the shoulder capsule and hold the large humeral head in the small glenoid: supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (lateral rotation) and subscapularis (medial rotation) - remembered as SITS.
They compress the joint while the deltoid and other prime movers act. Supraspinatus tendinopathy and tears, often from impingement under the coraco-acromial arch, are among the commonest causes of shoulder pain; the cuff is weakest superiorly and inferiorly is unprotected, so dislocations usually go anteroinferiorly.

Adductor pollicis.description:
Fan-shaped muscle deep in the palm with an oblique head (capitate and bases of the second and third metacarpals) and a transverse head (shaft of the third metacarpal), converging on the ulnar sesamoid and base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
It adducts the thumb and gives power to the pinch and key grips. It is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; its weakness in ulnar palsy makes the patient flex the thumb interphalangeal joint (flexor pollicis longus, median nerve) when gripping paper - Froment's sign.

Articularis genus muscle.description: Small, flat bundles from the lower anterior surface of the femur (deep to vastus intermedius) to the suprapatellar bursa. It pulls the bursa up during knee extension so it is not trapped between the patella and femur. Supplied by the femoral nerve.

Patellar ligament.description:
Strong, flat continuation of the quadriceps tendon from the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity; the patella is a sesamoid bone in this tendon. Tapping it elicits the knee jerk (L3-L4).
Its central third with bone blocks is a common graft for ACL reconstruction; overuse causes patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee), and traction on the tibial tuberosity in adolescents causes Osgood-Schlatter disease.

Occipital lobe.description:
The posterior lobe of each cerebral hemisphere, resting on the tentorium cerebelli. On the medial surface it is bounded by the parieto-occipital sulcus and divided by the calcarine sulcus into the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below; the primary visual cortex (area 17, striate cortex) lines the calcarine sulcus, surrounded by visual association cortex.
It is supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery, with the occipital pole in a watershed with the middle cerebral artery. Infarction causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.

Hypophysis.description:
The pituitary gland: a pea-sized endocrine gland in the sella turcica of the sphenoid, connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum and roofed by the diaphragma sellae, with the optic chiasm just above and the cavernous sinuses on either side.
The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) secretes GH, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH under the control of hypothalamic hormones carried by the hypophyseal portal veins; the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) releases ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamic neurons. A pituitary macroadenoma growing upward compresses the chiasm, classically causing bitemporal hemianopia.

Parathyroid glands.description:
Usually four small endocrine glands on the back of the thyroid: the superior pair from the fourth pharyngeal pouch, fairly constant near the cricothyroid junction, and the inferior pair from the third pouch (with the thymus), more variable and sometimes ectopic in the mediastinum.
Their chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone, which raises serum calcium by bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and activation of vitamin D. They are supplied mainly by the inferior thyroid arteries and are at risk at thyroidectomy (post-operative hypocalcaemia).

Tracheobronchial tree.description:
The branching airways from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles. The trachea divides at the carina (about T4-T5) into the right main bronchus - shorter, wider and more vertical, so aspirated objects usually go right - and the left main bronchus, which passes under the aortic arch. These divide into lobar (secondary) and segmental (tertiary) bronchi, each segmental bronchus supplying a bronchopulmonary segment.
The conducting zone is lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium; cartilage plates disappear at the bronchioles, whose walls are held open by the pull of the surrounding lung.

Extrahepatic bile ducts.description:
The ducts carrying bile from the liver to the duodenum: the right and left hepatic ducts join in the porta hepatis to form the common hepatic duct, which receives the cystic duct from the gallbladder to become the common bile duct. This runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum, behind the first part of the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas, and joins the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, opening at the major duodenal papilla controlled by the sphincter of Oddi.
Stones impacted in the common bile duct cause obstructive jaundice; the cystohepatic (Calot) triangle is dissected in cholecystectomy to identify the cystic artery and duct.

Radiocarpal joint.description:
The wrist joint proper: an ellipsoid synovial joint between the distal radius and the articular disc of the distal radio-ulnar joint above and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum below. It allows flexion, extension, abduction (radial deviation) and adduction (ulnar deviation), with circumduction; rotation happens at the radio-ulnar joints instead.
It is stabilised by palmar and dorsal radiocarpal and collateral ligaments. A fall on the outstretched hand typically fractures the distal radius or the scaphoid rather than dislocating this joint.

Crico-arytenoid joint.description: Synovial joint between the base of each arytenoid cartilage and the upper border of the cricoid lamina. Its rocking and gliding movements, produced by the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, open and close the vocal folds. It can be fixed by rheumatoid arthritis or dislocated by intubation, mimicking vocal fold paralysis.

Root of pulmonary trunk.description: The beginning of the pulmonary trunk at the pulmonary valve, where it leaves the conus arteriosus (infundibulum) of the right ventricle in front of and to the left of the aortic root. The three pulmonary sinuses lie behind the valve cusps.

Posterior funiculus.description:
The dorsal column of the spinal cord white matter, between the posterior horns: the fasciculus gracilis (from the lower body) medially and, above T6, the fasciculus cuneatus (from the upper body) laterally. It carries ipsilateral fine touch, vibration and conscious proprioception to the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the medulla, from which the medial lemniscus crosses.
Its damage (vitamin B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis) causes sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg sign.

Anterolateral fasciculus.description: The anterolateral system of the spinal cord white matter, mainly the spinothalamic tracts. It carries pain, temperature and crude touch from the opposite side of the body, the fibres having crossed within one or two segments in the anterior white commissure. Hemisection of the cord therefore causes contralateral loss of pain and temperature (Brown-Séquard syndrome); anterolateral cordotomy was used to relieve intractable pain.

Gluteal region.description: The buttock, from the iliac crest to the gluteal fold, formed by the gluteal muscles over the back of the pelvis and hip. The sciatic nerve runs through its lower medial quadrant, so intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant (or ventrogluteal site) to avoid it and the superior gluteal nerve.

Posterior region of knee.description: The back of the knee, overlying the popliteal fossa: a diamond-shaped space bounded by biceps femoris above laterally, semimembranosus and semitendinosus above medially, and the two heads of gastrocnemius below. It contains, from superficial to deep, the tibial and common fibular nerves, popliteal vein and popliteal artery (whose pulse is felt deep in the fossa with the knee flexed), plus popliteal lymph nodes; a Baker cyst presents here.

Greater supraclavicular fossa.description: The depression above the middle third of the clavicle, overlying the lower posterior triangle of the neck (omoclavicular triangle). The trunks of the brachial plexus and the third part of the subclavian artery lie deep to it - the site of supraclavicular plexus block and of palpation for enlarged supraclavicular nodes.

Heel region.description: The back and underside of the heel, over the calcaneus. Its thick fat pad of fibrous septa absorbs heel-strike forces; the plantar fascia arises from the medial calcaneal tubercle (the site of pain in plantar fasciitis), and the Achilles tendon inserts on the posterior surface.

Parotideomasseteric region.description: The region of the lateral face over the parotid gland and masseter, in front of the ear and behind the anterior border of masseter. The facial nerve branches fan out through the parotid, and the parotid duct crosses masseter a finger's breadth below the zygomatic arch before piercing buccinator.
